summary: This note is a PubMed record for a 2009 meta-analysis by Rong Su, James Rounds, and Patrick Ian Armstrong in Psychology Bulletin, examining sex differences in vocational interests. The study pooled technical manuals for 47 interest inventories covering 503,188 respondents, measuring Holland's categories, Prediger's Things-People and Data-Ideas dimensions, and STEM interest areas. The main finding is that men prefer working with things and women prefer working with people, with a large effect size, and the authors suggest interests may play a critical role in gendered occupational choices and STEM gender disparity. The surrounding page navigation and account boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: A 2009 meta-analysis of 47 interest inventories finding men prefer things and women prefer people, with implications for gendered occupational and STEM choices.
key_facts: The paper is 'Men and things, women and people: a meta-analysis of sex differences in interests' by Rong Su, James Rounds, and Patrick Ian Armstrong, published in Psychol Bull in 2009 Nov;135(6):859-884.
The DOI of the paper is 10.1037/a0017364 and the PMID is 19883140.
The meta-analysis used technical manuals for 47 interest inventories, yielding 503,188 respondents.
Men prefer working with things and women prefer working with people, producing a large effect size (d = 0.93) on the Things-People dimension.
Men showed stronger Realistic (d = 0.84) and Investigative (d = 0.26) interests.
Women showed stronger Artistic (d = -0.35), Social (d = -0.68), and Conventional (d = -0.33) interests.
Sex differences favoring men were found for engineering (d = 1.11), science (d = 0.36), and mathematics (d = 0.34) interests.
Average effect sizes varied across interest inventories, ranging from 0.08 to 0.79.
The quality of interest inventories, based on professional reputation, was not differentially related to the magnitude of sex differences.
Moderators of effect sizes included interest inventory item development strategy, scoring method, theoretical framework, and sample variables of age and cohort.
Application of some item development strategies can substantially reduce sex differences.
The study suggests interests may play a critical role in gendered occupational choices and gender disparity in the STEM fields.
The paper is classified as a Meta-Analysis and Comparative Study, with Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't also listed.
Full text is linked through the American Psychological Association.
